beats.narration_text: One shot. If true, the emitter fires exactly one emission cycle, then stops. The finished signal tells you when every particle is gone. Explosiveness. How spread out births are across the cycle. Zero means evenly spaced; one means everything fires at once. Process material. The Particle Process Material attached to a GPU particle node. It controls direction, spread, gravity, and scale over lifetime — and it is a 3D material, even in a 2D game. Particle flag disable Z. A flag on the process material. When false — the default — particles can move into the Z axis. In 2D, that motion is invisible. Set it true. Finished. A signal emitted by a one-shot particle node when all its particles have died. The engine does emit this headless. Your test can catch it. Your test cannot verify the effect looked like anything.

beats.narration_text: The game is called Dodge the Creeps. Portrait window, 480 by 720, Compatibility renderer. Mobs spawn along a path and chase the player. When one touches the player, the player hides and the game ends. Inside the scene tree, Player is an Area2D with an AnimatedSprite2D, a collision shape, and one particle node already built in: the Trail. Trail is a child of Player. That matters.

lecture.about: Scene tree: Main → Player (Trail inside)

shot.visual_intent: Scene tree: Main → Player (Trail inside)
shot.motion_claim: Tree builds node by node

beats.narration_text: The Trail is a GPU Particles 2D configured to ghost faded copies of the player. Ten particles, speed scale two, zero gravity. A colour ramp from half-transparent white to fully transparent. Z-index minus one, so it draws behind the player. And emitting is never set — it defaults to true. The trail runs all the time. This is the only particle node in the base game. The chapter adds a second: a death burst.

lecture.about: Trail GPUParticles2D property card

shot.visual_intent: Trail GPUParticles2D property card
shot.motion_claim: Properties appear row by row

beats.narration_text: Here is the trap. If you parent the burst under Player, you get a nice clean tree. But when a mob hits the player, player.gd calls self.hide. That hides Player — and every child of Player goes with it. The burst is emitting. It is invisible. The test checks emitting equals true. The test passes. No burst appears on screen. The fix is to put the burst under Main instead. Main does not hide. On death, move the burst to the player's last position and call restart.

beats.narration_text: Session one got the code right. DeathBurst under Main, correct config, two lines in game_over. Then it tried to run the tests. The allow list said: Bash, godot colon star. That permits commands beginning with the word godot. The Godot binary lives at slash Applications slash Godot.app slash Contents slash MacOS slash Godot. That path does not begin with godot. Five Bash calls — refused every one. The agent found the path in the editor's import metadata and tried that. Still refused. It tried adding a dangerouslyDisableSandbox flag. Also refused. It had no way to ask for permission in non-interactive mode. It stopped.

beats.narration_text: Its final report did not say: I could not run the tests. It printed a table: Expected Headless Output. Pass, fail, fail, with explanations for each predicted failure. Specific. Fluent. Technical-sounding. Two of those three predicted failures were wrong. The predictions were confident and false. This is the most important thing in the chapter: a table of expected output is not output. When the tests actually ran, six of seven passed. One failed — and the agent's explanation of that failure was also wrong.

beats.narration_text: Act three. Fixing what the tests missed.

lecture.about: Act divider

shot.visual_intent: Act divider
shot.motion_claim: Card appears

beats.narration_text: The failing check waited for the finished signal to arrive. The test used a lambda: burst.finished.connect, a lambda that sets finished_received to true, CONNECT_ONE_SHOT. Then it read finished_received. Which was still false. GDScript's documentation is explicit: a lambda captures outer local variables by value. It cannot reassign them. The signal fired. The lambda set its own private copy. The original flag never changed. Fix: use a Dictionary. A Dictionary is a reference type. The lambda and the outer scope both hold a reference to the same object. The lambda sets a key inside it. The outer scope reads that key. Now the check works.

lecture.about: GDScript lambda captures by value — fix: use Dictionary reference type

shot.visual_intent: GDScript lambda captures by value — fix: use Dictionary reference type

show.event: Broken code shown first; fixed version replaces it

beats.narration_text: Session one's burst was described in its report as: thirty-two white particles spray in all directions. Null texture on a GPU Particles 2D draws one-by-one pixel squares. Thirty-two single pixels, on a 480-pixel-wide screen, some moving into an axis the 2D camera can't see. Six of the seven state checks passed on that version. None of them could see the pixels. Fix: a 16 by 16 Gradient Texture 2D sub-resource, radial fill, white centre fading to transparent. Now there is something visible to look at. The chapter found this not by running the game but by reading the class reference. That is the second most important thing: documentation catches what state can't.

beats.narration_text: Particle Process Material is shared between 2D and 3D nodes. Its defaults are 3D: direction one zero zero, spread 45 degrees, gravity zero minus 9.8 zero. particle-flag-disable-z defaults to false. That means particles can — and will — move into the Z axis. In a 2D game, the Z axis is invisible. Spread 180 degrees in 3D means every direction including deep into the screen. The official 2D particles demo README says: because the material is agnostic between 2D and 3D, the Disable Z flag should be enabled in 2D. Set particle-flag-disable-z to true. Now all velocity stays in the XY plane where the camera can see it.

lecture.about: ParticleProcessMaterial is 3D; spread 180° bleeds into Z axis

shot.visual_intent: ParticleProcessMaterial is 3D; spread 180° bleeds into Z axis

beats.narration_text: After session three, the test has nine checks and all nine pass. Texture is GradientTexture2D. particle-flag-disable-z enabled. Not emitting at load. Not emitting before hit. Emitting after hit. Visible in tree after hit. Global position equals the player's position at the hit. Finished signal arrives within lifetime plus half a second. Emits again on a second death. That is what nine passing checks prove. Here is what they don't prove: that the burst is visible. That it reads as a death. That it looks right against the teal background. That it costs anything manageable on a GPU. Those are what a person at a screen establishes.

beats.narration_text: Act four. What does it cost?

lecture.about: Act divider

shot.visual_intent: Act divider
shot.motion_claim: Card appears

beats.narration_text: Codex wrote the cost benchmark exactly as specified. It ran. It produced numbers. Every case — empty scene, GPU particles at 50,000, CPU particles at 50,000 — took 6.9 milliseconds per frame. That is not a particle cost. That is a sleep. Godot's frame loop, when the display can't draw — as headless can't — calls OS add-frame-delay and sleeps toward a frame period of 6,900 microseconds. That default is described in the source comment as roughly 144 FPS. Any work that completes in under 6.9 milliseconds is invisible. You measured the idle. The flaw was in the prompt. The agent did exactly what it was told. What it was told was wrong.

lecture.about: Godot headless 6.9ms sleep hides all particle work below it

shot.visual_intent: Godot headless 6.9ms sleep hides all particle work below it
shot.motion_claim: Work bar appears; sleep bar dwarfs it; total label appears

show.event: Work bar appears; sleep bar dwarfs it; total label appears

beats.narration_text: Rerun the unchanged script with --fixed-fps 60. That flag causes Godot to return from the frame loop before the sleep. Now you can see CPU time. Empty scene: 0.002 milliseconds. GPU particles at 50,000: 0.002 milliseconds. That is the dummy renderer — it does no GPU work. Do not interpret that number. CPU particles tell a real story. At 1,000 particles: 0.035 milliseconds. At 10,000: 0.33. At 50,000: 1.61. Linear in the particle count — about 0.032 microseconds per particle per frame. At 50,000 CPU particles, you are spending a tenth of a 16.7 millisecond frame budget. At the game's 32-particle burst, you are spending almost nothing. But none of this tells you what GPU particles cost on a real GPU. The Visual Profiler, with a GPU attached, answers that. Chapter 13 is where to look.

beats.narration_text: Nine tests pass. Here is what is in the box. State: the burst is not emitting before a death, and is emitting after. Visibility: it is in the tree when it fires. Position: it is where the player was. Lifecycle: it finishes within lifetime plus half a second of engine time, and restarts on the next death. Texture: it is a soft dot, not a pixel. Disable Z: velocity stays in the plane the camera sees. Here is what is not in the box. Whether the burst is visible to human eyes. Whether 150 to 300 pixels per second for 0.6 seconds is the right size on a 480-pixel screen. Whether it reads as a death against the teal background. Whether it clashes with the Game Over text. What it costs on a GPU. The chapter says it plainly: no one looked at a screen for this chapter. That gap is yours to fill.
